items.passage: A local church tax in Germany had long gone unenforced, so economist Nadja Dwenger and colleagues treated the sizable payments members made anyway as intrinsically motivated. When the researchers then warned some members of enforcement or offered others rewards for paying, that voluntary compliance did not decline, suggesting that such incentives are ______ intrinsic motivation.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: When the researchers added warnings and rewards, “that voluntary compliance did not decline.” The incentives worked alongside what members already paid of their own accord instead of pushing that motive aside, so the two kinds of motivation can exist together: the incentives are compatible with intrinsic motivation.

A.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that the incentives depend on intrinsic motivation; the text describes the incentives and the voluntary compliance existing side by side.

B.why_wrong: If the incentives were a substitute for intrinsic motivation, they would take its place and voluntary compliance would fall, but the text says that compliance “did not decline.”

D.why_wrong: A catalyst for intrinsic motivation would make it grow, but the text says only that voluntary compliance “did not decline,” not that the warnings and rewards increased it.

sources.what: Dwenger, Kleven, Rasul, Rincke, AEJ: Economic Policy 8(3) 2016, abstract: German local church tax historically relied on zero deterrence, so baseline compliance is intrinsically motivated; field experiment incentivized compliance through deterrence or rewards; intrinsic compliance is substantial, driven partly by duty-to-comply preferences; no crowd-out between extrinsic and intrinsic motivations (abstract read via the OpenAlex record of this DOI)

items.notes: Subject: social science (behavioral public finance). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (incentives were added and voluntary compliance did not fall, so the two motives coexist; then the relation word). Ranks (freq.txt, rarest content word): contingent 17,762; substitute 9,221; compatible 23,068; catalyst not listed. Near miss: a catalyst for (the text says only that voluntary compliance did not decline, not that it grew). Treatments simplified to rewards or warnings of enforcement; the passage does not say how members were contacted.

fixes: authors: named three of four (Rincke left out), now 'economist Nadja Dwenger and colleagues' (AEA abstract page lists Dwenger, Kleven, Rasul, Rincke)

'payments rose' under both treatments is not in the abstract (full text not reachable); softened to what the abstract states, no crowd-out: 'that voluntary compliance did not decline'; explanation and why_wrong A, B, D rewritten to match
review.note: Core claim (zero-deterrence church tax, deterrence or reward treatments, no crowd-out) checked on the AEA abstract page.

band7.why: Target 6 by plan and it meets it. Raw ranks contingent on 17,762; a substitute for 9,221; compatible with 23,068; a catalyst for unseen (3 of 4 past 10,000). Two steps (incentives added, voluntary compliance unchanged, so the motives coexist), key paraphrased away from the passage, catalyst for a near miss that fails on one feature (growth vs no loss).

items.subtype: Blank completion: phrase options (a/an + noun + preposition)
items.passage: For years, variations in the oxygen isotope ratios of stalagmites from Chinese caves were widely interpreted as ______ the quantity of rain delivered by the East Asian summer monsoon. Geoscientists Barbara Maher and Roy Thompson challenged that interpretation in 2012, arguing that the variations reflect shifts in the source of the moisture rather than changes in the amount of precipitation.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Maher and Thompson “challenged that interpretation,” arguing that the variations reflect “shifts in the source of the moisture rather than changes in the amount of precipitation.” The interpretation they challenged must therefore have tied the variations to the amount of rain, treating them as a measure, or gauge, of “the quantity of rain delivered by the East Asian summer monsoon.”

B.recipe: reversal: trait of the wrong party (ANT)
B.why_wrong: Treating the variations as independent of the amount of rain is Maher and Thompson’s position, not the earlier interpretation they “challenged.”

C.why_wrong: Isotope ratios in cave formations could not have produced the monsoon’s rain; the earlier reading treated the ratios as recording rainfall, not causing it.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that anyone thought the variations held back how much rain fell; the dispute is over what the isotope record measures.

sources.what: Maher, Thompson, Journal of Quaternary Science 27 (2012), abstract: oxygen isotope variations in Chinese stalagmites have been widely interpreted as a record of the amount of East Asian summer monsoonal rainfall; the variations cannot be accounted for by summer rainfall changes but instead reflect changes in moisture source

items.notes: Subject: natural science (paleoclimatology). Key letter A. Steps: 2 (the blank is the received view; the challenge says rather than the amount of rainfall, so the received view treated the ratios as measuring it). Band-7 B3 move used: blank on the view being challenged, with the challengers' trait (independent of) as a reversal. Ranks: gauge 16,357; independent 3,829; cause 715; hindrance 14,036. A constraint on was replaced in review: in geoscience usage a proxy that provides a constraint on rainfall measures it, a second reading close to the key.

fixes: option D a constraint on replaced by a hindrance to: 'a constraint on' has a technical sense (data that puts bounds on an estimate) that a science-literate student could read as a measure of rainfall, close to the key; why_wrong D and notes updated
review.note: Core claim (stalagmite oxygen isotopes widely read as monsoon rainfall amount; Maher and Thompson 2012 argue moisture source instead) checked on the OpenAlex abstract of the DOI.

band7.why: Target 6 by plan. Raw ranks a gauge of 16,357; independent of 3,829; a cause of 715; a hindrance to 14,036: 2 of 4 past 10,000. The B3 move inside B6 (blank on the challenged view, the challengers' trait independent of as the wrong-party reversal) carries it to band 6; a cause of is the soft distractor.

items.passage: Legal historian Emily Kadens argues that the story of a medieval “law merchant,” a body of commercial law supposedly created and enforced by merchants themselves, has an unusually ______ hold on scholars interested in private ordering. Although numerous historical studies have demonstrated its falsity, the story still appears regularly in scholarship as an accurate portrayal of medieval commerce.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The text says that “numerous historical studies have demonstrated its falsity,” yet “the story still appears regularly in scholarship as an accurate portrayal of medieval commerce.” A belief that keeps its grip on scholars even after repeated refutation has a persistent, stubborn hold, so the hold is tenacious.

A.why_wrong: A precarious hold would be insecure and likely to slip, as one might expect of a story whose “falsity” numerous studies have demonstrated, but the story “still appears regularly in scholarship as an accurate portrayal of medieval commerce,” so its hold has stayed firm.

B.why_wrong: Apocryphal means of doubtful truth. It describes the story itself, whose “falsity” studies have demonstrated, not the hold the story has on scholars, who still present it “as an accurate portrayal of medieval commerce.”

C.why_wrong: Equivocal means uncertain or ambiguous, but the story still appears in scholarship “as an accurate portrayal of medieval commerce,” which shows a firm rather than an uncertain hold.

sources.what: Kadens, The Medieval Law Merchant: The Tyranny of a Construct, Journal of Legal Analysis 7 (2015), abstract: the story of a medieval law merchant has a strong hold on scholars interested in private ordering; despite numerous historical works demonstrating the falsity of the myth, it continues to be discussed regularly in scholarship as if it were an accurate portrayal of the past

items.notes: Subject: history and social science (legal history). Key letter D. Steps: 2 (refuted yet still treated as accurate, so the hold persists; then the trait word). Ranks: precarious 13,764; apocryphal 39,430; equivocal 24,700; tenacious 15,769. The gloss of the law merchant (law made and enforced by traders) is the standard description of the construct Kadens tests. Review: ephemeral replaced by precarious so that a wrong option also collocates with hold (precarious hold) and is the reading the concessive half invites.
band7_moves: all four options past rank 10,000, two past 20,000
clue phrased in a different register from the key (still appears in scholarship although its falsity has been demonstrated)
topic-echo trap that describes the myth rather than its hold (apocryphal)
collocating reversal built from the concessive half (precarious hold), added in review

fixes: option A ephemeral replaced by precarious: only the key collocated with hold (tenacious hold), so the item solved by collocation; precarious hold is a stock phrase and the trap the concessive 'Although ... falsity' half invites; why_wrong A and notes updated
review.note: Core claim (law merchant story keeps a strong hold on private-ordering scholars despite works showing it false) checked on the OpenAlex abstract of the DOI.

band7.why: After the fix: raw ranks precarious 13,764; apocryphal 39,430; equivocal 24,700; tenacious 15,769: 4 of 4 past 10,000, mean log 4.33. Concessive frame ('Although ... demonstrated its falsity, ... still appears'), two collocating options (tenacious hold, precarious hold) with the reversal built from the concessive half, and apocryphal names the passage's 'falsity' but describes the story, not its hold.

items.passage: Analyzing extensive supermarket scanner data and online prices, economist Daniel Levy and colleagues found that 9 is the most common final digit and that prices ending in 9 are less ______ than other prices. Such prices tend to persist for longer intervals, and the most frequent revisions are ones that preserve the 9 ending.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Prices ending in 9 “tend to persist for longer intervals,” and even when they are revised, “the most frequent revisions are ones that preserve the 9 ending.” Such prices resist change, so they are less mutable, or less likely to change, than other prices.

A.why_wrong: Remunerative means profitable. The sentence that follows the blank gives evidence about how rarely the prices change, not about how much money they bring in.

C.why_wrong: Sacrosanct means too important to be changed. Prices that hold longer and keep their 9 when revised are more sacrosanct than others, not less.

D.why_wrong: Ostentatious means showy. Nothing in the text concerns how prices ending in 9 display themselves; it reports how seldom they change.

sources.what: Levy, Lee, Chen, Kauffman, Bergen, Price Points and Price Rigidity, Review of Economics and Statistics 93(4) 2011, abstract: weekly scanner data and Internet data; 9 is the most frequent ending; the most common price changes keep the price endings at 9; 9-ending prices are less likely to change than non-9-ending prices; 9-ending contributes to price rigidity

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics of pricing). Key letter B. Steps: 2 (less + mutable; the evidence shows prices that resist change). Ranks: remunerative 31,748; mutable 50,138; sacrosanct not listed; ostentatious 20,698. Not the left-digit bias (live in two items): this is how often prices change. The abstract's result on the size of price changes is left out.
band7_moves: negation carried by a comparative (less ______) rather than stated outright
all four options past rank 20,000, one unseen in the corpus
reversal of the implied logic (sacrosanct) instead of a negation flip

fixes: authors: named three of five (Kauffman and Bergen left out), now 'economist Daniel Levy and colleagues' (OpenAlex record of the DOI)
review.note: Core claim (9 the commonest ending, 9-ending prices less likely to change, changes keep the 9) checked on the OpenAlex abstract.

band7.why: Raw ranks remunerative 31,748; mutable 50,138; sacrosanct unseen; ostentatious 20,698: 4 of 4 past 20,000, key past 50,000, rarest distractor unseen. Negation hidden in a comparative ('less ______', as d7807ec8 sanguine); one step is allowed because the vocabulary carries it. Sacrosanct is the reading a student gets by dropping 'less'.

items.passage:
The following text is from Owen Wister’s 1906 novel Lady Baltimore. The narrator is talking with Miss La Heu, whose dog, General, was recently killed by an automobile.

“Oh, his heart! General, listen to—” From habit she had turned to where her dog used to lie; and sudden pain swept over her face and was <u>mastered</u>. “Never mind!” she quickly resumed. “Please don’t speak about it. And you have a heart somewhere; for it was very nice in you to come in yesterday morning after—after the bridge.”
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “mastered” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Miss La Heu turns by habit to her dead dog’s spot, and “sudden pain swept over her face.” Right after that she says “Never mind!” and “quickly resumed” the conversation, so the pain was brought under control. In this context “mastered” means subdued.

B.why_wrong: To master a skill or subject is to learn it, but Miss La Heu is not learning her pain; she is bringing it under control so that she can go on talking.

C.why_wrong: The pain did show when it “swept over her face,” but “mastered” describes what happened next, when she controlled it and “quickly resumed” speaking, not its being revealed.

D.why_wrong: To tolerate pain is only to put up with it. “Mastered” goes further: Miss La Heu brings the pain under control, and right away she “quickly resumed” with “Never mind!”

sources.what: Owen Wister, Lady Baltimore (1906), Project Gutenberg eBook #1386: passage copied exactly (double hyphens set as closed em dashes); Miss La Heu's dog General was killed by an automobile earlier in the novel

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel). Key letter A. Exposed is a scene word, not a sense of mastered; the key is pinned by quickly resumed and Never mind. Target in a secondary sense (master = bring under control) against a real sense (Learned), a scene word that fits loosely (Exposed, from swept over her face) and a near miss (Tolerated). Ranks: subdued 3,813; learned 829 (learn); exposed 4,760; tolerated 13,186 (tolerate 11,533). Work not used in any official or bank item (grepped author and title). Review: Perfected (a sense of master that does not fit the sentence at all) replaced by Tolerated, a word that fits the scene and fails on one feature (putting up with pain vs bringing it under control), as Composure sits beside Constraint in 6557f7fc.

fixes: option D Perfected replaced by Tolerated: Learned and Perfected were both senses of master that make no sense with pain, so the item read easier than band 6; Tolerated fits the scene and fails on one feature (putting up with vs controlling); why_wrong D and notes updated; re-solved blind, Subdued the one defensible answer
review.note: Excerpt matches Gutenberg 1386 exactly (double hyphens as closed em dashes); General killed by an automobile at the drawbridge earlier in the novel, confirmed in the text.

band7.why: Target 6 by plan. Before the fix two distractors (Learned, Perfected) were senses of master that do not fit the sentence, so one look at 'pain ... was mastered' solved it (band 5 at most). After it, as the band-6 model 9b22bf7b: one real sense (Learned), one scene word (Exposed) and one near miss that fits the scene (Tolerated); options are common words, so not band 7.

items.passage: Harvestmen of the genus Prionostemma frequently lose legs to predators and cannot regenerate them, yet biologist Ignacio Escalante and colleagues showed that these arachnids make several ______ adjustments: in experiments, individuals that slowed sharply immediately after shedding legs modified their strides and posture, switched gaits, or even recruited legs normally used for sensing into locomotion, recovering their initial speed within two days.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: After shedding legs, the harvestmen “slowed sharply,” and then they “modified their strides and posture, switched gaits, or even recruited legs normally used for sensing into locomotion,” “recovering their initial speed within two days.” Adjustments that make up for a loss are compensatory.

A.why_wrong: Prophylactic means preventive, but the adjustments came after the legs were lost; they made up for the damage rather than heading it off.

B.why_wrong: Maladaptive means harmful to the animal, but the adjustments came with the harvestmen “recovering their initial speed within two days.”

D.why_wrong: Perfunctory means done carelessly or as a mere formality, yet the animals modified their strides, posture, and gaits, even changing which legs they walked on, and recovered their speed.

sources.what: Escalante, Badger, Elias, Rapid recovery of locomotor performance after leg loss in harvestmen, Scientific Reports 10 (2020), abstract: induced autotomy in Prionostemma; high leg loss in the field, no regeneration; immediate substantial drop in velocity; recovered initial performance after 2 days; post-autotomy changes in stride and postural kinematics; some changed gaits and/or recruited the sensory legs for locomotion

items.notes: Subject: natural science (biomechanics, arachnids). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (the adjustments follow a loss and restore speed, so they make up for it). Ranks: prophylactic 73,313; maladaptive not listed; compensatory 56,846; perfunctory 14,278. Leg loss in the wild is simplified to loss to predators (autotomy is an escape defense); a live spiny-mouse skin-shedding item is a different animal and premise (escape, not recovery).
band7_moves: colon and a list of described behaviors, key the abstract category they instantiate
all four options past rank 10,000, three past 50,000 or unseen
near-synonym distractor that fails on one feature (prophylactic: before rather than after the loss)

review.note: Core claim (Prionostemma harvestmen, no regeneration, speed recovered after 2 days through stride, posture and gait changes and use of sensory legs) checked on the PubMed abstract.

band7.why: Raw ranks prophylactic 73,313; maladaptive unseen; compensatory 56,846; perfunctory 14,278: 4 of 4 past 10,000, 3 past 50,000, key past 50,000. B4 recipe (colon and a described experiment, key the abstract category). Prophylactic is the near synonym that fails on one feature (before the loss, not after), and section 5 allows the other two to be plainly unsupported when rare, as here.

items.passage: Because storm clouds are short-lived and largely inaccessible, the microorganisms and organic compounds they contain have received little ______. Researcher Tina Šantl-Temkiv and colleagues circumvented this obstacle by analyzing hailstones from a single storm as natural samples of the cloud, identifying its bacterial community and nearly 3,000 distinct dissolved compounds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Storm clouds are “short-lived and largely inaccessible,” and the researchers “circumvented this obstacle” by analyzing hailstones “as natural samples of the cloud.” The obstacle is that the clouds are hard to study, so their contents have received little scrutiny, or close examination.

A.why_wrong: Publicity is public attention. The obstacle the researchers got around by sampling hailstones was the difficulty of studying the clouds, not a lack of public notice.

B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns how much the clouds’ contents vary; the problem it describes is that the clouds are hard to reach.

C.why_wrong: The text gives no reason to think the microorganisms lack protection; it explains why the clouds have been hard to sample.

sources.what: Santl-Temkiv et al., Hailstones: a window into the microbial and chemical inventory of a storm cloud, PLoS ONE 8 (2013), abstract: studies on these inaccessible and short-lived atmospheric habitats have been scarce; first comprehensive biogeochemical investigation of a storm cloud using hailstones as a natural sampling tool; molecular formulae of almost 3000 compounds in the dissolved organic matter; total and cultivable bacterial community

items.notes: Subject: natural science (atmospheric microbiology). Key letter D. Steps: 2 (little + the obstacle the second sentence removes). Ranks: publicity 12,049; variation 18,161; protection 2,739; scrutiny 5,667. Near miss: publicity (attention of the wrong kind).

review.note: Core claim (inaccessible, short-lived storm clouds little studied; hailstones as natural samples; almost 3,000 compounds) checked on the PubMed abstract.

items.passage: Lakota artist Dyani White Hawk’s Wopila, a monumental 2022 composition of half a million glass beads named for a Lakota expression of profound gratitude, presents Western abstract painting as ______ Indigenous artistic traditions. White Hawk has explained that the work honors generations of Lakota women whose abstraction helped nurture and guide Western painters.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: White Hawk says Wopila honors Lakota women “whose abstraction helped nurture and guide Western painters,” and the work is named for “profound gratitude.” If Indigenous abstraction helped shape Western painting, the work presents that painting as owing something to Indigenous artistic traditions: as indebted to them.

A.why_wrong: The work honors Lakota women for helping “nurture and guide” Western painters, so it presents Western abstraction as drawing on Indigenous art, not as opposed to it.

C.why_wrong: Comparable to would claim only a likeness between the two traditions, but the text claims influence: Lakota abstraction “helped nurture and guide” Western painters.

D.why_wrong: Western painters could hardly have been guided by Lakota abstraction if it were unknown to them; nothing in the text suggests that.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Dyani White Hawk: Sicangu Lakota artist; commissioned to create Wopila | Lineage (2022), a work of half a million glass bugle beads, for the 2022 Whitney Biennial; the title references the Lakota word for deep gratitude; she states the piece honors the lineage of Lakota women and their contributions to abstraction and the generations of practiced abstraction that helped nurture and guide the work of the Western artists inspired by it

items.notes: Subject: humanities (painting and beadwork). Key letter B. Steps: 2 (Lakota abstraction guided Western painters, and the work gives thanks, so Western abstraction owes it a debt). Ranks: opposed 6,009; indebted 11,122; comparable 16,254; unknown 1,536. Near miss: comparable to (likeness rather than influence). Full title Wopila | Lineage shortened to avoid the bar character. Replaces a Feliciano Centurión subject also taken by a wave-5 Central Ideas writer.

review.note: Core claim (Wopila | Lineage, 2022 Whitney Biennial, half a million glass beads, title from the Lakota word for deep gratitude, honors Lakota abstraction that helped guide Western artists) checked on Wikipedia. Two glass-bead artworks in one batch judged too close; item 12 (Liza Lou) was replaced, this one kept.

items.passage: Psychologists Kathryn Friedlander and Philip Fine characterize solving a British cryptic crossword as code-cracking detective work. A clue’s surface reading, the meaning it appears to have as an ordinary phrase, is intentionally ______, so experienced solvers learn to disregard it and search instead for grammatically coded instructions that, executed precisely, yield the single correct answer.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Solvers “learn to disregard” the surface reading and “search instead for grammatically coded instructions,” and the whole task is “code-cracking detective work.” A reading that must be set aside to reach the real answer is designed to mislead, so it is intentionally deceptive.

B.why_wrong: Redundant means unneeded because it repeats something. Solvers set the surface reading aside because it points away from the answer, not because it repeats the coded instructions.

C.why_wrong: A transparent reading would be clear and honest, but solvers must “disregard it” and look for hidden instructions instead.

D.why_wrong: The surface reading is “the meaning it appears to have as an ordinary phrase,” so it is everyday language, not technical language.

sources.what: Friedlander, Fine, The Grounded Expertise Components Approach in the Novel Area of Cryptic Crossword Solving, Frontiers in Psychology 7 (2016), abstract: the British cryptic crossword is an exercise in code-cracking detection work; solvers learn to ignore the superficial surface reading of the clue, which is phrased to be deliberately misleading, and look instead for a grammatical set of coded instructions which, if executed precisely, lead to the correct (and only) answer

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology of expertise). Key letter A. Steps: 2 (solvers must ignore the reading to find hidden instructions, so the reading misleads). Ranks: deceptive 17,391; redundant 44,163; transparent 7,165; technical 10,091.

review.note: Core claim (surface reading deliberately misleading, solvers ignore it for coded instructions) checked on the PubMed abstract.

items.passage: Bumble bees sometimes “rob” a flower, extracting nectar through a hole in its side without transporting pollen. Biologist Anne Leonard and colleagues found that on artificial flowers, a symmetric nectar guide pattern made legitimate visits more efficient for bees than robbing, so the pattern ______ robbing: bees visited flowers displaying it legitimately more often than they visited unpatterned ones.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The pattern “made legitimate visits more efficient for bees than robbing,” and bees “visited flowers displaying it legitimately more often.” By making the usual route to the nectar easier, the pattern made robbing less attractive: it discouraged robbing.

A.why_wrong: The pattern made legitimate visits, not robbing, the more efficient choice, so it did not reward robbing.

B.why_wrong: The text says only that bees visited patterned flowers legitimately “more often,” not that they stopped robbing them, so prevented overstates the effect: the pattern made robbing less common.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that the pattern hid robbing from view; the text describes how it changed the way bees took nectar.

sources.what: Leonard, Brent, Papaj, Floral nectar guide patterns discourage nectar robbing by bumble bees, PLoS ONE 8 (2013), abstract: bees sometimes extract nectar from a hole in the side of the flower without transporting pollen (nectar robbing); with artificial flowers, a symmetric nectar guide made legitimate visits more efficient for bees than robbing and increased the relative frequency of legitimate visits compared to flowers lacking nectar guides (Bombus impatiens)

items.notes: Subject: natural science (pollination ecology). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (the pattern makes the legitimate route more efficient, so robbing becomes less attractive; more often, not always). Ranks: rewarded 6,664; prevented 3,932; discouraged 8,224; disguised 7,583. Near miss: prevented (too strong). Replaces an earwig wing subject already claimed by another wave-5 writer.

fixes: why_wrong B reworded: 'more often' shows robbing became less common, not that some robbing provably continued
review.note: Core claim (symmetric nectar guide made legitimate visits more efficient than robbing and raised their relative frequency) checked on the PubMed abstract.

items.passage:
The following text is from Edith Somerville and Martin Ross’s 1899 short story “The Policy of the Closed Door.” Sally, a young woman, has fallen into a stream during a fox hunt.

He was off his horse and beside her with that uncanny quickness that Flurry <u>reserved</u> for moments of emergency, and, catching her by the arms, swung her on to the bank as easily as if she had been the kennel terrier.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “reserved” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Flurry shows “that uncanny quickness” only in “moments of emergency,” so it is something he keeps back for those occasions. In this context “reserved” means saved for a particular use.

A.why_wrong: To reserve a seat or table is to book it, but Flurry is not arranging anything in advance; the text describes a quickness he shows only when there is an emergency.

B.why_wrong: A reserved person is restrained in manner, but here Flurry moves with “uncanny quickness,” the opposite of holding back.

C.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that Flurry put off acting; he is “off his horse and beside her” at once.

sources.what: Somerville and Ross, Some Experiences of an Irish R.M. (1899), Project Gutenberg eBook #34630, story The Policy of the Closed Door (opening meet of the foxhounds; Sally's horse rolls in a stream): passage copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature (short story). Key letter D. Two senses of reserve (book, restrained in manner) and one unsupported word. Ranks: booked 20,875; restrained 5,774; delayed 5,951; saved 1,285. The Real Charlotte by the same authors is live in another item; this collection is not used anywhere (grepped title and story).

review.note: Excerpt matches Gutenberg 34630 exactly; story and context (Sally's horse rolls in the stream at the meet) confirmed in the text.

items.passage: When East Germany collapsed in 1989 and 1990, officers of its secret police, the Stasi, tore up many files by hand. Piecing those files back together has been a ______ task: more than a decade after the work began, a small team of archivists had fit together the scraps from only a few hundred of some 16,000 bags.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The text says that “more than a decade after the work began, a small team of archivists had fit together the scraps from only a few hundred of some 16,000 bags.” Work that moves this slowly and demands so much careful effort is a painstaking task.

A.why_wrong: A hasty task is done quickly, but after “more than a decade” the archivists had finished “only a few hundred” of the bags.

C.why_wrong: The files came from a “secret police,” but nothing suggests that the archivists’ work of piecing them back together is kept secret; the text describes how slowly that work goes.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that fitting the scraps together puts anyone at risk; it describes how long and slow the work is.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Stasi Records Agency, Reconstruction of destroyed files: as the archives were secured, Stasi officers whose shredders broke down tore files by hand and stuffed the pieces into bags; about 16,000 bags, each with 2,500 to 3,500 fragments, held by the agency; work began in the early 1990s and by early 2007 the contents of around 350 bags had been manually reconstructed by a small team

items.notes: Subject: history (East Germany, archives). Key letter B. Steps: 1 (a decade for a few hundred of 16,000 bags restates the slow, careful labor). Ranks: hasty 3,745; painstaking 22,230; secret 631; dangerous 1,553. Written in review to replace a Liza Lou beaded-kitchen item (second glass-bead artwork in the batch beside 08). Figures kept within both Wikipedia pages (Stasi Records Agency: work began in the early 1990s, about 350 bags done by hand by early 2007; Stasi: begun 1995, 327 bags after 13 years), so the passage says a few hundred after more than a decade. The jigsaw-puzzle framing of news reports is avoided.

fixes: item replaced: Liza Lou's beaded Kitchen was a second glass-bead artwork beside Dyani White Hawk's Wopila (08) and shared two distractors (secretive, profitable) with item 22; new subject Stasi file reconstruction (history), key kept at B, re-solved blind, claim appended to claims.txt with a WITHDRAWN line for Liza Lou
review.note: Core claim (files torn by hand, about 16,000 bags, a few hundred reconstructed by hand after more than a decade) checked on Wikipedia, Stasi Records Agency, and cross-checked against Wikipedia, Stasi.

items.passage: Korean painter Kim Tschang-yeul’s Event of Night, a painting of water droplets, received critical acclaim at the 1972 Salon de Mai in Paris. The painting ended a lengthy period of ______ for the artist. In a 1974 letter to fellow painter Park Seo-bo, Kim remarked that after a decade without a single exhibition, numerous shows had suddenly been scheduled.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Kim remarked that he had gone “a decade without a single exhibition” before the acclaim for Event of Night, after which “numerous shows had suddenly been scheduled.” Years without shows were years in which his work was little known, so the painting ended a period of obscurity.

A.why_wrong: Celebrity means fame, but before Event of Night Kim had gone “a decade without a single exhibition.”

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests Kim had been resting; the text says only that his work had not been shown.

D.why_wrong: The text mentions no quarrel or struggle with anyone; it describes a lack of exhibitions.

items.passage: Green lacewing larvae often camouflage themselves by carrying packets of debris on their backs. A larva in Early Cretaceous amber from Spain, described by paleontologist Ricardo Pérez-de la Fuente and colleagues, shows that this behavior is ______: more than 110 million years old, the fossil carries a dense packet of fern hairs in a basket of specialized bristles.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The fossil larva is “more than 110 million years old,” yet it already carries a packet of debris just as modern larvae do. The debris-carrying behavior therefore goes back a very long way: it is ancient.

B.why_wrong: A behavior found in a fossil “more than 110 million years old” is not recent.

C.why_wrong: The text describes one fossil and says that modern larvae “often” carry debris; nothing suggests the behavior is rare.

D.why_wrong: The text presents debris carrying as camouflage that helps larvae, not as something that harms them.

items.passage: Born in Barberton, South Africa, in 1982 and raised by her grandmother, artist Mary Sibande is the daughter of a domestic worker, and her mother’s experience shapes her art. In her sculptures, paintings, and photographs, Sibande often ______ women in that occupation, paying homage to domestic workers and seeking to give them a voice.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Sibande’s art is described as “paying homage to domestic workers and seeking to give them a voice.” Paying homage to people means showing them respect, so her work honors women in that occupation.

A.why_wrong: To mock domestic workers would be to ridicule them, the opposite of “paying homage” to them.

B.why_wrong: Domestic workers are hired by employers, but the text is about how Sibande portrays them in her art, not about employing anyone.

C.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that Sibande doubts or challenges these women; she seeks “to give them a voice.”

The following text is from Sheila Kaye-Smith’s 1921 novel Joanna Godden. Joanna, who owns a large farm, has just told her sister, Ellen, that she plans to sell it.

The colour <u>mounted</u> to Joanna’s face. She looked at her sister’s delicate, thoughtful face, with its air of quiet happiness. The room was full of sunshine, and Ellen was all in white.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “mounted” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: “The colour mounted to Joanna’s face” describes Joanna blushing: color moved up into her face. In this context “mounted” means rose.

A.why_wrong: One can mount, or organize, a campaign or an event, but color moving into a person’s face is not being organized.

C.why_wrong: A museum mounts, or displays, an exhibit, but here the color is moving up into Joanna’s face, not being put on show by someone.

D.why_wrong: A picture can be mounted, or attached, to a backing, but the sentence describes color rising in Joanna’s face, not anything being fastened.

items.passage:
The following text is from Mary Webb’s 1917 novel Gone to Earth. Edward Marston, a minister, has just come home, where his wife, Hazel, is waiting for him.

A new Hazel met him on the threshold, no longer timorous, deprecating, awkward, but gravely and sweetly maternal. She led him in. Tea was <u>laid</u> with the meticulous reverence of a sacrament.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “laid” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Hazel leads Edward in, and the tea is ready for him, arranged “with the meticulous reverence of a sacrament.” A table or meal that is laid has been set out, so “laid” means set.

A.why_wrong: A hen lays, or produces, eggs, but here the tea is being arranged for a meal, not produced by an animal.

B.why_wrong: To lay a bet is to wager, but nothing in the scene involves betting; the tea has been prepared for Edward.

D.why_wrong: To lay blame is to place it on someone, but the sentence describes how carefully the tea was arranged, not anyone being blamed.

items.passage:
The following text is from Fannie Hurst’s 1919 short story collection Humoresque. Sam and Clara are traveling by subway in New York City.

They let themselves be swept into the great surge of the underground river with all of the rather thick-skinned unsensitiveness to shoulder-to-shoulder contact which the Subway engenders. Swaying from straps in a locked train, which <u>tore</u> like a shriek through a tube whose sides sweated dampness, they talked in voices trained to compete with the roar.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “tore” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: The train moves “through a tube” so fast and loudly that Sam and Clara must talk “in voices trained to compete with the roar.” A train that tore through a tunnel raced through it, so “tore” means sped.

B.why_wrong: To tear paper or cloth to pieces is to shred it, but the train is not shredding anything; it is moving rapidly “through a tube.”

C.why_wrong: A person torn between two choices is divided, but the sentence describes a train rushing “through a tube,” not anyone caught between options.

D.why_wrong: A torn muscle is injured, but nothing in the scene is hurt; the word describes how the train moved.

sources.what: Fannie Hurst, Humoresque (1919), Project Gutenberg eBook #9864, story A Boob Spelled Backward (Sam and Clara head for the subway): passage copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature (short story). Key letter A. Ranks: sped 4,667; shredded 43,239 (shred 16,447); divided 3,268; injured 3,873. Screamed was rejected as a distractor because a train can scream through a tunnel. Collection not used anywhere; the source line names the collection because the story's first periodical date was not checked. Review: Ripped replaced by Shredded, since rip can itself mean to rush (a train that ripped through a tunnel), which made Ripped a second fit.

fixes: option B Ripped replaced by Shredded: rip also means to move fast ('ripped through the tube' reads naturally), a second defensible option; why_wrong B and notes updated

items.passage: Researchers Lorraine Maxwell, Mari Mitchell, and Gary Evans introduced loose parts suitable for construction to a preschool playground. The materials proved ______ constructive play: such activity increased in the areas where the parts had been placed, and children used the small enclosures they assembled for imaginative, dramatic games.

A.why_wrong: Constructive play “increased” where the parts were placed, so the materials helped it rather than harming it.

C.why_wrong: The loose parts were added to the playground by the researchers; nothing suggests they were taken from constructive play.

items.passage: On the slopes of Mount Kenya, most sorghum seeds are exchanged among relatives, so farmers’ seed networks largely follow kinship ties. Because members of the Mbeere dialect group seldom intermarry with the neighboring Chuka and Tharaka, researcher Vanesse Labeyrie and colleagues discovered, seed exchanges between the Mbeere and those communities are ______.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

A.why_wrong: Since seeds pass mainly between relatives and the groups “seldom intermarry,” exchanges between them would be rare, not frequent.

items.passage: A large log-jam repeatedly forms where Texas’s San Antonio River is shifting its course into a channel called Elm Bayou. Geographer Jonathan Phillips determined, however, that the jam did not ______ that shift. Instead, wood accumulates at the site because of the narrow, stable channels created where the river’s flow divides.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Phillips found that the jam is not behind the river’s shift: “Instead, wood accumulates at the site because of the narrow, stable channels created where the river’s flow divides.” The jam is a result of conditions at the site rather than the cause of the shift, so it did not trigger that shift.

items.passage: Household recipe books from early modern England have often been described as the work of women alone. Historian Elaine Leong argues, however, that most were ______ projects. The notebook of medical recipes that Mary Cholmeley brought to Yorkshire when she married Henry Fairfax in 1627, for instance, was supplemented for decades by Mary, Henry, their children, and other relatives.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Leong’s view is set against the idea that the books were “the work of women alone,” and her example shows one notebook “supplemented for decades by Mary, Henry, their children, and other relatives.” Books compiled by many family members working together were collective projects.

A.recipe: reversal: trait of the wrong party (ANT)
A.why_wrong: Solitary work is what the earlier description implies (“the work of women alone”); Leong argues “however” against it, and her example involves a whole family.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns what the books cost; it is about who wrote in them.

D.why_wrong: The notebook was kept and added to by a family for its own use; nothing suggests the books were made for sale.
